text: A single pilot team with one SRE embedded in it works well precisely because it's small — one service, one set of SLOs, engineers who all know each other. The moment ten services want that same support, the structure has to change deliberately, or it fails quietly: either every product team hires its own SRE and duplicates tooling with no consistency, or the practice stays confined to the pilot team and never actually scales. This is a real organizational design problem, not just a headcount question.

In the embedded model, SRE engineers are assigned directly to one product team, working alongside its developers day to day. The advantage is deep context: an embedded SRE understands this service's specific failure modes and traffic patterns because they live inside it. The real tradeoff is breadth and leverage — practices and tooling tend to diverge between embedded SREs on different teams unless something actively prevents that, and an embedded SRE can drift into being just the ops person for that team.

In the centralized model, SRE sits as its own organization — often like a platform team — providing shared tooling, standards, and sometimes an escalation layer across many services at once. The advantage is leverage: one SLO dashboard, one incident-response investment, one postmortem standard, applied everywhere instead of rebuilt N times. The real tradeoff is distance — a centralized org can lose the close context that makes an embedded SRE effective on any one service, and product teams can start seeing SRE as an outside auditor rather than a partner.

In practice, organizations that scale SRE well tend to land on a hybrid: a central team builds and maintains the shared platform — SLO tooling, incident tooling, postmortem standards — while product-aligned SRE presence, sometimes a rotating assignment, applies that platform to each service's real operational reality. This isn't indecision; it's matching each part of the practice to the structure that actually serves it, since shared infrastructure benefits from central leverage while service-specific judgment benefits from proximity.

Scaling isn't only an org-chart question, either. As service count grows, self-service tooling becomes essential — a team defining its own SLO through a documented platform instead of needing a dedicated SRE to hand-build one, because linear headcount growth with service count doesn't work forever. That closes this chapter: a pilot that proves the practice, an error budget that negotiates the real tradeoff, a culture that's actually lived, and a structure built to grow with the organization instead of breaking under it.
